40 years of cognitive architectures: core cognitive abilities
and practical applications
Iuliia Kotseruba 1 · John K. Tsotsos 1
Published online: 28 July 2018
© The Author(s) 2018
Abstract
In this paper we present a broad overview of the last 40 years of research on cognitive
architectures. To date, the number of existing architectures has reached several hundred, but
most of the existing surveys do not reﬂect this growth and instead focus on a handful of
well-established architectures. In this survey we aim to provide a more inclusive and high-
level overview of the research on cognitive architectures. Our ﬁnal set of 84 architectures
includes 49 that are still actively developed, and borrow from a diverse set of disciplines,
spanning areas from psychoanalysis to neuroscience. To keep the length of this paper within
reasonable limits we discuss only the core cognitive abilities, such as perception, attention
mechanisms, action selection, memory, learning, reasoning and metareasoning. In order to
assess the breadth of practical applications of cognitive architectures we present information
on over 900 practical projects implemented using the cognitive architectures in our list. We
use various visualization techniques to highlight the overall trends in the development of
the ﬁeld. In addition to summarizing the current state-of-the-art in the cognitive architecture
research, this survey describes a variety of methods and ideas that have been tried and their
relative success in modeling human cognitive abilities, as well as which aspects of cognitive
behavior need more research with respect to their mechanistic counterparts and thus can
further inform how cognitive science might progress.
Keywords Survey · Cognitive architectures · Perception · Attention · Cognitive abilities ·
Practical applications

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=theoretical+frameworks+for+machine+agency+and+moral+responsibility+attribution&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"title\": [\"Self-Good Desire and the Moral Agency of Artificial Intelligence :A Criterion of Life Integrity for Responsibility Attribution\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The increasing autonomy of artificial intelligence has intensified the \\\"responsibility gap\\\" and the debate over AI moral agency. Existing accounts commonly appeal to rational capacity, sentience, or functional performance, but these criteria do not fully explain either the motivational basis for taking norms as reasons or the conditions under which a subject can bear ultimate moral responsibility. Drawing on the framework developed in On Self-Good Desire, this paper argues that \\\"self-good desire\\\" (sishan yuqiu) is a motivationally necessary condition of full moral agency. It denotes an intrinsic, selfnurturing motivational structure through which a living subject maintains its existence, improves its condition, and pursues its development, unfolding into eleven root desires: self-preservation, self-care, self-enrichment, self-beautification, self-joy, self-compassion, self-reflection, self-confidence, selfstrengthening, self-respect, and freedom. \\\"Life integrity\\\" here does not reduce moral agency to a particular biological substrate; rather, it refers to an integrated organization of self-maintenance, felt value, diachronic identity, and self-concern. Self-good desire is not sufficient for full moral agency, which also requires normative understanding, behavioral control, and responsibility-bearing capacity. On this account, current AI systems can represent norms and simulate forms of moral reasoning, yet there is presently insufficient warrant to attribute to them endogenous needs, first-person experience, enduring self-concern, or genuinely self-generated stakes. They therefore should not be treated as full moral agents. When AI systems cause harm, ultimate moral responsibility should ordinarily remain with human and institutional actors and be allocated by reference to control, causal contribution, benefit, foreseeability, and duties of care.
